papers.title: Preparedness of health facilities for emergency neonatal care in West Cameroon: a cross-sectional study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368724 v1

summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional survey of 185 health facilities in five districts of Cameroon's West Region measures how prepared they are to deliver emergency neonatal care, using a WHO/UNFPA assessment framework.
summary.plain: Babies who fall sick or have trouble breathing soon after birth need fast, skilled care, and many die when it is missing. This study checked 185 health clinics and hospitals in part of western Cameroon to see whether they had the staff, equipment, and written rules to handle such emergencies. Overall, most were poorly prepared: the average score was about 51%, and about 69% of facilities scored in the low range.
summary.why: It gives concrete local figures on gaps such as missing incubators, resuscitation bags, and trained staff, which can guide where limited resources should go. The text does not report whether preparedness is linked to actual newborn deaths, so its direct impact on outcomes is not shown here.
summary.background:
- Neonatal mortality: deaths of newborns in their first month of life.
- Emergency neonatal care (EmNC): urgent care for newborns, such as breathing support, antibiotics, and treatment for jaundice or low temperature.
- Health facility preparedness: whether a site has the trained people, working equipment, supplies, and written procedures needed for a task.
- SARA framework: a WHO/UNFPA tool for assessing health service availability and readiness.
- Integrated health centre (CSI): a basic primary-care facility in Cameroon's health system; CMA is a larger hospital-type facility.
- Cross-sectional study: a one-time snapshot survey, which shows associations but not cause and effect.

papers.abstract: Background Limited access to quality emergency neonatal care (EmNC) contributes to high neonatal mortality in Cameroon, yet data on facility readiness in the West Region are scarce. This study assessed the preparedness of health facilities for EmNC in this region. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study from March to May 2026 in five health districts of the West Region. All eligible facilities were included. Data were collected through a questionnaire for health professionals and an observation checklist adapted from the WHO/UNFPA SARA framework. Preparedness scores were classified as high ([≥]80%), moderate (60-79%) or low (<60%). Results We surveyed 185 health facilities (74.1% integrated health centers, 63.2% rural, 49.7% public) and 243 health professionals. The mean preparedness score was 51.1%; 11.4% of facilities had a high level of preparedness, 20.0% moderate and 68.6% low. At least one qualified staff member was present in 64.3% of facilities, and written neonatal protocols in 45.9%. Essential equipment was scarce: bag-valve-mask (13.0%), functional incubator (19.5%), newborn transport equipment (13.5%), phototherapy unit (10.8%) and defibrillator (7.6%), whereas vitamin K was widely available (95.7%). Mean scores were highest in private for-profit facilities (64.9%) compared with public (47.7%) and private non-profit facilities (45.1%), in district hospitals (66.2%) and CMAs (66.0%) compared with integrated health centers (45.9%), and in urban areas (60.9%) compared with rural (48.6%) and semi-urban areas (40.4%). Conclusions Most health facilities in the West Region are poorly prepared for newborn emergencies. Priorities include essential equipment with maintenance systems, qualified staff, written protocols and regular training, especially in integrated health centers and rural areas.

papers.title: Place or placeholder? AlphaEarth satellite embeddings did not detectably improve weekly dengue forecasts in four countries
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368794 v1

summary.one_liner: A retrospective test of whether AlphaEarth satellite embeddings improve weekly district dengue forecasts in Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Taiwan, with location-only controls to check whether any gain is just district recognition.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a set of satellite-derived numbers describing each district helps predict how many dengue cases will occur there in the coming one or four weeks. The authors tested this on about 6,900 districts across four countries from 2020 to 2024, and also checked whether any benefit came merely from the model recognising each place. They found no significant improvement after statistical correction, and several small losses.
summary.why: Satellite-based environmental summaries are increasingly used in disease forecasting, so it matters whether they add real predictive value beyond simply knowing where a place is. The paper's main contribution is a careful control design, and its finding is limited to these settings and this model type.
summary.background:
- Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease; weekly case counts by district are the forecast target.
- Forecast error here is measured by a weighted interval score, where lower is better and it reflects both the central estimate and the uncertainty range.
- AlphaEarth embeddings are compressed numerical summaries of satellite imagery for each location; they are not themselves measurements of weather or cases.
- A location control is an input that only identifies a district, so any gain from embeddings can be compared against what place identity alone provides.
- Gradient boosting is a standard machine-learning method that builds many decision trees in sequence.
- Diebold-Mariano tests compare forecast accuracy between two models; the Holm correction adjusts for running many comparisons; an equivalence margin of ±1% defines how small a difference counts as no meaningful effect.
- Held-out places and future years are tests of whether a model works on unseen regions or later time periods.

papers.abstract: Background. Some recent disease forecasts use satellite embeddings (numbers summarising places). A model may use them only as a placeholder, recognising districts and their usual dengue levels without learning about the environment. We asked whether AlphaEarth embeddings improve weekly district dengue forecasts and whether gains go beyond such recognition. Methods. We retrospectively forecast cases one and four weeks ahead in 6,909 districts of Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Taiwan (OpenDengue, 2020-2024) with gradient boosting. In 14 comparisons across future years and held-out places, we measured how embeddings changed the weighted interval score, with and without a location control (an input that only identifies a district), to test whether location alone explains gains. We used Diebold-Mariano tests, the Holm correction and a +/-1% equivalence margin set after the first Brazil and Peru results. Findings. No comparison showed a significant gain after correction. Six showed losses: five small (-0.42% to -0.68%) and one with Taiwan held out (-18.3%; absolute -0.0037). Only Colombia's held-out-states loss (-0.52%) stayed significant under two stricter checks and a check for cases hidden in zero-filled weeks. In 8 comparisons (5 under the stricter checks), any gain or loss was shown to be smaller than 1% of forecast error. This margin is roughly Brazil's gain from all non-case inputs combined. In exploratory analyses, embeddings alone predicted district burden in unseen states. Without case history, neither coordinates nor embeddings helped detectably in Brazil's held-out states; both hurt in Colombia's. In Brazil's future years, coordinates cut error by 3.3% (1.7 to 4.9); embeddings added nothing detectable. Interpretation. Embeddings partly showed which districts usually have more dengue, but in Brazil and Colombia other non-case inputs already held most of it. With case history they added no detectable accuracy; without it, evidence was inconclusive. Embeddings should be tested against location-only controls in held-out places.

papers.title: Proteogenomic analysis provides insights into the effect of physical activity on cancers
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.25.26368973 v1

summary.background:
- Mendelian randomization: uses genetic variants as stand-ins to test whether a factor causes an outcome, reducing confounding from lifestyle and other influences.
- GWAS summary statistics: published results from genome-wide association studies, which show how common genetic variants relate to a trait, used here without access to individual-level data.
- Proteome-wide: testing many blood proteins (here 2,940) one by one.
- Plasma proteins: proteins circulating in blood, measured as biomarkers of tissue activity.
- FDR (false discovery rate): a correction for the many simultaneous tests, with FDR<0.05 used as the significance threshold.
- Accelerometer-based measures: wearable motion sensors, compared with self-reported activity.
- Two-stage design: Stage 1 links activity to proteins; Stage 2 links proteins to cancer.
summary.one_liner: A two-stage proteome-wide Mendelian randomization study tests whether genetically predicted physical activity changes plasma protein levels and whether those proteins in turn affect risk of several site-specific cancers.
summary.plain: Past studies have linked more physical activity with lower rates of several cancers, but the biological route by which this happens is poorly understood. This paper uses genetic data from large population studies as a kind of natural experiment to look for blood proteins that sit between activity and cancer. The authors report many activity-protein links and a smaller set of proteins that also show effects on cancer risk.
summary.why: Identifying specific blood proteins that might carry the protective effect of exercise could point to targets for later study. The text is a summary only, so the strength of the causal claims and the validity of the cancer links cannot be judged from it; the prostate cancer example is presented as illustrative.

papers.abstract: Background. Increased physical activity (PA) has been associated with decreased risk of several cancers in epidemiologic studies, but the intermediate molecular mechanisms remains poorly characterized. Methods. Leveraging genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for 22 self-reported and accelerometer-based PA measures, plasma levels of 2,940 proteins (N = 34,557), and multiple site-specific cancers, we performed a two-stage proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. In Stage 1, we estimated the effects of each PA measure on plasma protein levels and in Stage 2, we evaluated the effects of PA-associated proteins on cancer risk. Results. We identified 687 PA-protein associations involving 503 unique proteins at FDR<0.05. Across 80 PA-responsive proteins curated from intervention-based studies, we nominally replicated 83% using our MR approach. Approximately 40% of PA-associated proteins were differentially expressed in response to exercise in transcriptomic datasets primarily localizing to muscle tissues, and in immune cell populations. In stage 2, 213 (of 503) PA-related proteins demonstrated significant effects on at least one cancer (FDR<0.05) highlighting them as proteomic intermediates of the effect of PA on cancer. For example, for prostate cancer (PCa), we observed that reductions in sedentary time and increases in light-intensity activity were associated with higher MSMB and lower TNF levels, which in turn reduced PCa risk. Conclusions. This study applies a two-stage Mendelian randomization framework to link PA, circulating proteins, and cancer risk, enhancing biological interpretation of epidemiologic PA-cancer associations and nominating a focused set of PA-associated proteins as potential targets for further investigation.

papers.title: Prenatal exposure to semi-volatile organic compounds and early childhood sleep duration
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.25.26368881 v1

summary.background:
- Semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs): chemicals that slowly leave plastics, coatings, pesticides and fuels and float in indoor air and dust.
- Groups named: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (from combustion such as smoke), phthalates (plasticizers), and organophosphate esters (flame retardants and plasticizers).
- Silicone wristbands worn for several days act as passive air samplers that collect these chemicals.
- Prospective pregnancy cohort: families followed from pregnancy onward, with exposure measured before birth.
- Generalized linear mixed-effects models: statistical models that account for repeated measures within families and for adjustment variables such as child age and race.
- Multiplicative change: a ratio; 0.77 means expected sleep is about 23% lower per the exposure measured, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.61 to 0.95 (a range of plausible values).
- Mixture analysis: looks at several chemicals together rather than one at a time.
summary.one_liner: In a North Carolina pregnancy cohort of 147 children aged 2–24 months, prenatal wristband measures of semi-volatile organic compounds were associated with shorter parent-reported sleep among 2-month-olds but largely not at older ages.
summary.plain:
This study asks whether chemicals that pregnant women are exposed to from everyday products, such as plastics, flame retardants and fuels, affect how long babies sleep. Mothers wore silicone wristbands that soak up airborne chemicals during each trimester, and parents later reported their children's sleep. Among 2-month-old babies, higher prenatal levels of several of these chemical groups were linked to less sleep over day, night and total 24 hours, while the links were mostly absent in older infants.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Sleep is central to early brain and body development, and chemical exposures before birth are a modifiable concern, so a link like this is worth tracking. The text reports associations only and relies on parent-reported sleep, so it does not show that the chemicals cause the sleep changes; the authors themselves call for studies of broader sleep health.

papers.abstract: Background: Adequate sleep duration is critical for early childhood development; however, environmental determinants of sleep during this period remain understudied. Objective: We evaluated associations between prenatal exposure to semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs) and parent-reported sleep duration among 147 children 2-24 months of age. Methods: Mothers in Project HOPE 1000, a prospective pregnancy cohort in central North Carolina, wore silicone wristbands for 5 days during each trimester, and 117 SVOCs were quantified. Generalized linear mixed-effects models were adjusted for child age, race, ethnicity, and an exposure-age interaction term. Results: At least 70% of wristbands had detectable levels of 36 SVOCs. Among 2-month-olds, higher prenatal exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, phthalates, and organophosphate esters was associated with decreased sleep duration across daytime, nighttime, and total sleep over a 24-hour period (e.g., benzyl butyl phthalate exposure was associated with lower expected nighttime sleep duration (Multiplicative Change: 0.77, 95% Confidence Interval: 0.61, 0.95). Results among 2-month-olds were similar when exposure was assessed as a mixture. Associations were largely null at older ages across all sleep outcomes. Significance: Prenatal SVOC exposure may have significant impacts on sleep duration during early infancy. Future studies should assess how these differences relate to broader measures of sleep health.

papers.title: Sources of protein in UK adults following contemporary plant-based diets: findings from the Feeding the Future (FEED) Study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368579 v1

summary.one_liner: Cross-sectional analysis of the UK Feeding the Future (FEED) cohort (n=6,113) quantifying the food sources of protein across omnivore, flexitarian, pescatarian, vegetarian and vegan diets and the share of each group meeting the estimated average requirement (EAR) for protein, with and without under-reporters excluded.
summary.plain:
This study looks at where protein comes from in the diets of about 6,100 UK adults who eat in different ways, from meat-eaters to vegans. The researchers estimated how much of each person's protein came from different food groups, and how many people got less protein than a basic daily need. Few people fell short, and most of the apparent shortfall among vegetarians and vegans disappeared once people who likely under-reported their food intake were removed.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Plant-based eating is becoming more common, and people often ask whether it provides enough protein. This paper gives a detailed, food-by-food picture for a large UK group, which is useful for nutrition guidance. The text reports only dietary questionnaire data, so it describes associations and reported intake rather than what people actually absorbed or how their health fared.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Protein is built from amino acids and is needed for growth, repair and maintenance of tissue.
- The estimated average requirement (EAR) is the intake level expected to meet the needs of half of people in a group; it is not a personal target.
- Cross-sectional means data were collected at one point in time, so no cause and effect can be drawn.
- Food frequency questionnaire: a survey asking how often people eat listed foods, used here to estimate intake.
- Under-reporters: people whose recorded energy intake looks implausibly low compared with their likely needs, suggesting incomplete reporting.
- Plant-based meat alternatives and dairy alternatives are manufactured products (for example, tofu-like or soy-based foods); legumes and pulses are beans, peas and lentils.

papers.abstract: Objective To identify and quantify sources of protein intake in United Kingdom (UK) adults following different diets, and assess how these sources contribute to meeting protein requirements. Design Cross-sectional analysis of the Feeding the Future Study (FEED), a UK cohort recruited in 2022-2023. Dietary intake was assessed using an online food frequency questionnaire. We calculated the percentage contribution of food groups to daily protein intake, and the proportion of participants meeting the estimated average requirement (EAR) for protein, with and without exclusion of under-reporters. Setting A contemporary cohort of UK adults. Participants 6,113 adults: 1,540 omnivores, 1,322 flexitarians, 547 pescatarians, 1,212 vegetarians, and 1,492 vegans. Results Grains contributed 10-30% of total protein intake across all groups. Dairy contributed 12.9-14.2% in non-vegan groups, while plant-based dairy alternatives contributed less in vegans (7%), mainly from soy milk (4.3%). Other major contributors (>10%) were meat for omnivores (33.0%) and flexitarians (13.5%); fish for pescatarians (14.9%); plant-based meat alternatives for vegetarians (12.0%); and plant-based meat alternatives (15.0%), legumes and pulses (10.5%), and nuts and seeds (10.5%) for vegans. The proportion below the protein EAR ranged from 1.9% in omnivores to 14.0% in vegans, falling to 0.01% and 3.6% respectively, after excluding under-reporters. Conclusions Grains were a major contributor to protein intake across all diet groups, as was dairy in all non-vegan groups. Protein sources were more varied in non-omnivorous groups, particularly vegans. Few participants fell below the protein EAR and the higher proportions among vegetarians and vegans were largely attenuated after excluding under-reporters.

papers.title: Meta-analysis of Sequencing Data Identifies Candidate Endometrial Cancer Susceptibility Genes
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368185 v1

summary.background:
- Endometrial cancer is a cancer of the lining of the womb (uterus).
- Genes are instructions for building proteins; a "variant" is a spelling change in a gene.
- Protein-truncating variants (PTVs) cut a protein short and often disable it; missense variants (MSVs) swap one building block for another, and only some are predicted to be harmful.
- Burden tests compare how often rare variants in a gene appear in cases versus controls.
- RR (relative risk) compares how much more likely someone with the variant is to develop the cancer; wide confidence intervals signal uncertainty.
- Exome-wide significance is a strict statistical threshold used to correct for testing thousands of genes at once.
- Mismatch repair genes (MSH2, MSH6, MLH1) are already known to raise risk of Lynch syndrome-related cancers.
summary.one_liner: A burden-test meta-analysis of rare protein-truncating and missense variants in 2,675 endometrial cancer cases and 160,654 controls from UK Biobank and 100,000 Genomes Project, reporting known and candidate susceptibility genes.
summary.plain: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological cancer in wealthy countries, but its inherited causes are only partly known. The researchers looked at rare genetic changes across the protein-coding part of the genome in thousands of people with and without the cancer, asking which genes carry changes linked to higher risk. They confirmed the known risk genes MSH6, MLH1, MSH2 and PTEN and reported about 19 further genes, such as PHKG2, that they describe as candidates needing confirmation.
summary.why: Identifying inherited risk genes could eventually help find people at higher risk for screening or counselling. The text itself frames the new genes as preliminary candidates that still need replication in other studies, so their clinical value is not yet established.

papers.abstract: BackgroundEndometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in high-income countries, yet its genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. While pathogenic variants in mismatch repair genes are well-established contributors, the role of rare variants in other genes has not been systematically characterized. MethodsWe evaluated associations between rare genetic variants and endometrial cancer risk based on 2,675 cases and 160,654 controls from the UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project. Gene-level associations were assessed using burden tests, with protein-truncating variants (PTVs) and missense variants (MSVs) predicted to be deleterious analysed separately. ResultsEndometrial cancer (EC) risk associations were observed for three established EC susceptibility genes in the rare PTV analysis: MSH6 (RR = 36.6, 95% CI 25.9-51.8), MLH1 (RR = 52.5, 95% CI 21.3-129.4) and MSH2 (RR = 13.0, 95% CI 6.0-28.2). In the rare MSV analysis, PTEN was also significantly associated with EC risk (RR = 9.7, 95% CI 4.0-23.7). Beyond these established susceptibility genes, exome-wide significance was observed for 19 additional genes in the PTV analysis, including PHKG2 (RR = 29.8, 95% CI 9.6-92.8), and eight additional genes in the MSV analysis. ConclusionThis study identifies novel candidate genes associated with endometrial cancer risk, providing a foundation for future replication studies.

papers.title: Improving Prediction of Patient-Reported Health Outcomes Among Older Adults With Diabetes Across Diverse Populations Through Transfer Learning
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.26368865 v1

summary.background:
- Diabetes: a long-term condition in which blood sugar regulation is impaired; common in older adults.
- Prediction model: a statistical formula that estimates the chance of an outcome from risk factors such as age or clinical measures.
- Transfer learning: reusing information from related datasets to improve a model built on a smaller target dataset.
- Transportability: whether a model that works in one population still works in another.
- AUC: a 0 to 1 score for how well a model separates people who will have an outcome from those who will not; higher is better.
- Brier score: a measure of how close predicted probabilities are to what actually happened; lower is better.
- Bootstrap resampling: repeatedly resampling the data to estimate how uncertain a result is.
- Patient-reported outcomes: health measures reported by participants themselves rather than by clinicians.
summary.one_liner: A regression-based transfer learning approach was tested for predicting patient-reported health outcomes in older adults with diabetes, borrowing information from international aging cohorts (Gateway) and race/ethnicity groups in the RAND HRS, with gains evaluated by AUC and Brier score.
summary.plain: Prediction models built on one group of people often work less well on another group that differs in background or health setting. This paper tests whether a method called transfer learning, which borrows useful information from other related datasets, can make predictions for older adults with diabetes more accurate. The authors compared it with models built only on the target group and with models pooling all the data, across eight international cohorts and four race/ethnicity groups in a US study.
summary.why: Many prediction tools are developed on one population and may not transfer to others, which matters for fairness and for public health planning. The reported gains are small (about 0.1% to 3.1% in AUC), and the text itself describes them as modest, so the practical value is still an open question rather than a settled result.

papers.abstract: Population heterogeneity challenges the transportability of prediction models. Transfer learning may improve prediction through information borrowing, but its utility across population settings remains unclear. We evaluated a regression-based transfer learning framework across international aging cohorts (Gateway) and race/ethnicity groups within the RAND Health and Retirement Study (RAND HRS). Gateway included 19,879 adults with diabetes from eight cohorts, while RAND HRS included 3,926 participants across four race/ethnicity groups. Prediction models for patient-reported health outcomes were developed using demographic and clinical risk factors. Transfer learning was compared with target-only and pooled models using AUC and Brier score, with bootstrap resampling to assess uncertainty. Transfer learning improved prediction in 75% (6/8) of Gateway cohorts, with AUC gains of 0.1%-0.6%, and in all four RAND HRS race/ethnicity groups, with gains of 0.8%-3.1%. Improvements were greater and more consistent across within-cohort groups. These findings demonstrate the potential of regression-based transfer learning to improve prediction across heterogeneous populations. Information borrowing from sufficiently transferable external data may enhance prediction performance and provide meaningful public health benefits, even when improvements are modest, particularly in large population-based cohorts.

papers.title: Disease-anchored organ aging clocks enable multi-organ risk profiling from routine labs
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.22.26368688 v1

summary.background:
- Biological age: an estimate of how well body systems are functioning, which can differ from chronological age.
- Organ clocks: models that estimate the biological age of a specific organ (e.g., heart, kidney) from blood measurements.
- Proteomics: measuring large numbers of proteins in blood; costly and not routine.
- Routine laboratory tests: common blood tests (e.g., cholesterol, glucose, liver enzymes) done in standard clinical care.
- Frozen coefficients: the model's fitted weights are fixed after training and then applied unchanged to new cohorts.
- Negative control: random protein panels of matching size are used to check that results are not just due to panel size.
- Cohorts: UK Biobank (training), NHANES (US) and JMDC (Japan) (external tests).
- Clinical risk scores: standard tools that combine factors such as age and sex to estimate disease risk.
summary.one_liner: The paper trains organ-specific "aging clocks" on first onset of each organ's disease using routine blood lab tests from UK Biobank, freezes the coefficients, and tests whether they track own-organ disease risk in NHANES (US) and JMDC (Japan) cohorts.
summary.plain: Doctors can estimate how old a person's organs are behaving, not just their calendar age, by looking at blood markers. Existing methods of doing this need expensive protein measurements and are trained on age rather than disease. This paper builds organ "clocks" trained directly on when each organ's disease first appears, using ordinary lab tests, and then checks whether they flag the right organ's disease.
summary.why: The approach aims to make organ-level risk estimates possible from routine blood tests rather than specialised proteomics, which could matter for screening. The text reports that the frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in a second country's cohort, predicted own-organ disease in a third, and added information beyond current organ clocks to clinical risk scores; whether this improves care is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: Organ clocks estimate the biological age of organs from blood, but current clocks assign tissue-enriched proteins to organs and train on chronological age, which requires proteomics and does not yield organ-specific disease risk. In the UK Biobank, we trained organ clocks on first onset of disease of each organ using routine laboratory tests and froze the coefficients. Under an age label, organ-clock readouts arose equally in size-matched random protein panels; with a disease label, clocks selected their own organ's proteins and predicted their own organ's diseases. Defining extreme aging by multiples of disease risk concentrated flags on own-organ disease. Frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in the US NHANES cohort, predicted first onset of own-organ disease in the Japanese JMDC cohort and added more information to clinical risk scores than current organ clocks. Trained once where disease follow-up exists, organ clocks can be used wherever routine laboratory tests are measured.

papers.title: Epidemiology of Cardiac Structure and Function Among African Caribbeans in Tobago: A Population-based Cohort Study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368418 v1

summary.background:
- Heart failure: the heart does not pump or fill well enough to meet the body's needs.
- Echocardiography: an ultrasound scan of the heart.
- Left ventricle: the main pumping chamber; "LV mass index" measures how much muscle it has, relative to body size.
- Concentric remodeling: the heart wall thickens without the chamber enlarging, a common early change linked to high blood pressure.
- Diastolic dysfunction: stiffness that makes the heart fill poorly between beats.
- Ejection fraction (LVEF): the share of blood pumped out each beat; below 50% is generally considered reduced.
- Global longitudinal strain (GLS): a measure of how much the heart muscle stretches and squeezes; less negative values indicate weaker function.
- E/e' ratio and E/A ratio: ultrasound-based estimates of filling pressure and filling pattern.
- Stages A–C of heart failure: A is at risk without symptoms, B has structural changes without symptoms, C has symptoms.
- Population-based cohort: a study drawing a general community sample rather than hospital patients.
summary.one_liner: A population-based echocardiography study of 924 African Caribbean adults in Tobago describing the prevalence of left ventricular structural abnormalities, diastolic dysfunction, and reduced systolic and strain measures, stratified by sex, age, and heart failure stage.
summary.plain: Heart failure often develops after the heart's walls thicken or its filling and pumping function start to change, and people of African ancestry are at higher risk for it. This study scanned the hearts of 924 adults in Tobago using ultrasound (echocardiography) to see how common these early changes are. It found that most participants had an abnormal heart shape or thickened walls, and that women and older adults had more of these structural problems and filling difficulties than men and younger adults.
summary.why: Little was previously known about heart structure and function in people of African Caribbean descent in Tobago, so these prevalence figures give local health planners a baseline. The sex and age patterns may help guide cardiovascular prevention priorities, though the text does not show whether these findings change outcomes or care.

papers.abstract: BackgroundIndividuals of African genetic ancestry are at high risk for heart failure (HF), which is often preceded by cardiac structural and functional abnormalities. Nevertheless, little is known about cardiac structure and function among Afro-Caribbeans residing in Tobago. This study aimed to investigate the epidemiology of cardiac structure and function among African Caribbeans in Tobago. MethodsA total of 924 participants (41-83 years) underwent clinical evaluation and transthoracic echocardiography. Images were analyzed for left ventricular (LV) mass index (MI), left atrial volume index, diastolic dysfunction (DD), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e' ratio, E/A ratio, and other echocardiographic measures. Cardiac structure and function were evaluated by age, sex, and HF stage. ResultsThe mean age was 61.7 years, with 61.4% women, 47.8% obesity, and 20.2% diabetes. Average systolic blood pressure was approximately 140 mmHg, and 76.7% had hypertension. Abnormal LV geometry was present in 77.1% of participants, predominantly concentric remodeling (69.5%). The prevalence of DD was 13.4%, LVEF <50% was 1.5%, and abnormal GLS ([≤]-18%) was 5.2%. Women had significantly higher E/e' ratios and a higher prevalence of Stage A and Stage B HF, whereas men had a higher prevalence of symptomatic (Stage C) HF. Participants aged 65-83 years had significantly higher E/e' ratio, concentric remodeling, and LV hypertrophy than those aged 41-57 years. ConclusionsWomen and older adults have higher LV structural abnormalities and DD than men and younger adults. These results will be helpful to inform public health priorities related to cardiovascular health in Tobago.

papers.title: Improving UK Biobank algorithms for Parkinson's disease ascertainment using drug claims
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368409 v1

summary.background:
- UK Biobank: a large research database of health records and measurements from roughly half a million UK volunteers.
- Ascertainment: working out who has a condition, based on the records available.
- Misclassification: counting people with the wrong status, e.g. missing true cases or including people with similar conditions.
- Incidence: the rate of new cases over time.
- Parkinsonism: a group of movement symptoms that can have causes other than Parkinson's disease.
- Primary care data: records from family doctor (general practitioner) visits, available for only about 45% of participants here.
- Anti-PD drugs: medications such as levodopa commonly prescribed for Parkinson's; prescription records can hint at a diagnosis earlier than hospital records do.
summary.one_liner: Compares three ways of identifying Parkinson's disease cases in UK Biobank (hospital/death records, GP diagnoses, and a new drug-prescription-based algorithm) and how each choice changes incidence estimates and associations with sex, walking speed and mortality.
summary.plain: Researchers using a large UK health database often need to know which people have Parkinson's disease, but the database does not record this cleanly. This paper tests three ways of spotting cases: using hospital and death records, using family doctor diagnoses, and using a new method based on anti-Parkinson drug prescriptions. The authors found that the hospital-and-death-records approach missed about 20% of cases compared with the drug-based method and underestimated incidence by 36% against UK reference rates.
summary.why: Choices about how cases are identified can change study results, so this matters for anyone analysing Parkinson's risk factors in UK Biobank. The text does not show how far the drug-based method will hold up in other datasets, and it reports only the comparisons summarised in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Background: Accurate ascertainment of Parkinson's disease (PD) is a major challenge in large-scale epidemiological studies. The UK Biobank (UKB) is widely used for PD research, but ascertainment based on hospital and death records may result in misclassification and delayed PD diagnoses. Objectives: We compared different strategies for ascertaining PD in the UKB, and examined their impact on incidence and associations with risk factors and mortality. Methods: We compared PD ascertained through hospital and death records (ADO-PD) to two approaches that rely on primary care data available for ~45% of participants: diagnoses from general practitioner consultations (Clinical-PD); a novel drug-based algorithm (Drug-PD). We compared incidence, age at diagnosis, and associations with sex, walking speed, and mortality across all algorithms. Results: ADO-PD identified ~20% fewer prevalent and incident cases than Drug-PD over 15y of follow-up, and estimated age at diagnosis to be 4.2y (median) later than age at anti-PD drugs initiation. ADO-PD identified never treated participants or with other causes of parkinsonism as PD patients. While Drug-PD yielded incidence rates consistent with UK reference rates, ADO-PD underestimated incidence by 36% compared to reference rates. Associations with sex, walking speed, and mortality were significantly different for ADO-PD compared to Drug-PD. Clinical-PD and Drug-PD yielded similar findings, although Clinical-PD included patients with other causes of parkinsonism. Conclusions: We draw attention to methodological issues regarding PD ascertainment in the UKB and their consequences. These results can help inform strategies for PD ascertainment by combining multiple data sources, thereby improving the validity of epidemiological analyses.

papers.title: Personal HbA1c trajectories and incident diabetes: association, prediction and observability in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368578 v1

summary.background:
- HbA1c: a blood test reflecting average blood sugar over roughly the previous two to three months; a diagnostic threshold marks diabetes.
- Incident diabetes: diabetes that develops during follow-up, not present at the start.
- Prospective cohort: a group of people followed over time, with measurements taken repeatedly.
- Linear mixed model: a statistical model that estimates each person's typical level and rate of change while borrowing information across people.
- Cross-fitting: fitting model parameters on other participants to avoid overfitting to the person being predicted.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a method ranks people who will and will not develop the condition; 0.5 is chance.
- Transformer: a neural network architecture, here trained on the lab sequences, used as a comparison method.
- Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process: a model of random fluctuations that drift back toward an average and are correlated over time, used to mimic biological noise.
- Odds ratio per SD: how much the odds of diabetes change for each standard-deviation increase in a measure.
summary.one_liner: In English older adults (ELSA), individual HbA1c trajectories gave modest adjusted association with incident diabetes but did not improve prediction beyond baseline HbA1c, and a drift model suggests personal slopes are hard to recover from sparse measurements.
summary.plain: This study asks whether tracking a person's blood sugar marker (HbA1c) over several years predicts who will develop diabetes, better than a single test result. Using repeated measurements from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, the researchers found that a person's personal upward or downward trend was linked to later diabetes after adjustment, but adding these trend features did not clearly improve prediction overall. They also found that slow natural fluctuations make individual trends hard to pin down when tests are spaced years apart.
summary.why: It bears on how doctors might use repeated routine lab results rather than a single snapshot, and on the limits of such data for personal risk estimates. The text is an observational secondary analysis of one cohort, so its findings are measured and not a basis for changing clinical practice.

papers.abstract: Background. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a snapshot: a single measurement interpreted against a population threshold. Repeated (longitudinal) measurements, however, may reveal an individual's typical level and how it changes over time. Extracting this information is challenging when measurements are sparse and biological fluctuations may resemble sustained changes. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), we investigated whether individual glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) trajectories improved the prediction of incident diabetes beyond the most recent measurement, whether they were associated with incident diabetes, and how reliably they could be estimated. Methods. In this secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, we analysed venous HbA1c measured approximately every four years in ELSA, with a longer final interval of about seven years. A linear mixed model estimated each person's usual HbA1c level and rate of change (personal slope) from their measurements before each diabetes-free health visit, with model parameters estimated in other participants (cross-fitting). We derived four longitudinal features: deviation from the person's usual level, personal slope, change since the last measurement, and the forecast probability that the next HbA1c reaches the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. We evaluated the associations of these features with incident diabetes and their incremental predictive value beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors in internal, cross-fitted validation, compared predictive performance with a self-supervised Transformer, and modelled within-person variation as serially correlated drift (an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) to assess how reliably personal slopes can be recovered under different measurement schedules. Results. The analysis included 5,828 diabetes-free baseline visits from 3,603 participants, of which 234 were followed by incident diabetes. Neither the engineered longitudinal features nor a Transformer that also used additional clinical variables improved discrimination beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors (difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, {Delta}AUC, -0.002 to +0.010; all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] including zero). The estimated personal slope was nevertheless associated with incident diabetes after adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age and other clinical factors (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] 1.18, 95% CI 1.02--1.36, and 1.39, 1.11--1.74, among visits with at least two earlier HbA1c values), whereas deviation from the person's usual level was not (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.81--1.21). In the drift model, serially correlated fluctuations accounted for 77--81% of residual within-person variance, although the estimated temporal structure was sensitive to the treatment of the first HbA1c values at or above the diagnostic threshold. Under this model, persistent individual trends were difficult to distinguish from slowly varying fluctuations: with the intercept-slope correlation set to zero, estimated and underlying slopes correlated weakly for four-yearly measurements over up to 12 years (r [≤] 0.26), and more frequent measurements improved this little. Conclusions. Estimated personal HbA1c slopes carried adjusted prognostic information beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical factors, but longitudinal features, including those learned by a Transformer, did not clearly improve prediction. The drift model suggests that slowly varying within-person fluctuations may limit the reliable estimation of individual slopes from sparse measurements, and that longer observation histories are more informative than more frequent measurement. Whether personal laboratory histories improve prediction depends not only on their association with disease, but also on how reliably individual change can be recovered from the available measurements.

papers.title: Depressive Symptom Trajectories and Incident Cognitive Impairment by Outcome Ascertainment
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368449 v1

summary.background:
- Cohort study: following a group of people over time and recording who develops an outcome.
- Depressive symptom trajectories: groups of people with similar patterns of depression scores over time (e.g., persistently low, persistently high, worsening, remitting), identified statistically.
- Incident cognitive impairment: new memory or thinking problems that appear during follow-up.
- Ascertainment rigor: how carefully a condition is identified, from self-report up to a clinical expert consensus diagnosis (HCAP is a standardized cognitive assessment protocol).
- Hazard ratio (HR) and odds ratio (OR): measures of how much more likely an outcome is in one group than another; values above 1 mean higher risk.
- Meta-analysis and meta-regression: combining results across studies, and testing whether study features explain differences between them.
- Mild cognitive impairment (MCI): a stage between normal ageing and dementia.
summary.one_liner: In four harmonized national aging cohorts (91,043 adults aged 50+), depressive symptom trajectories were associated with incident cognitive impairment more strongly when outcomes were ascertained with more rigorous, clinically adjudicated methods, with a meta-regression exploring ascertainment rigor as a moderator of heterogeneity.
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether the link between long-term depression symptoms and later memory or thinking decline in older adults depends on how that decline is measured. They pooled data from aging studies in China, the US, England and Europe and found that when cognitive problems were judged by self-report, the link was weak or inconsistent across countries. When judged by a full clinical diagnosis, depression-related risk appeared for every non-low symptom pattern, and the effect grew with each step up in measurement rigor.
summary.why: It suggests that differences in past estimates of depression as a dementia risk factor may partly reflect how outcomes were measured, which matters for prevention trials and burden forecasts. The authors note the meta-regression is exploratory and based on only five levels, so the pattern should be checked in other data before being relied on.

papers.abstract: Importance: Dementia prevention frameworks treat depression as a leading modifiable risk factor, but cohort estimates of the association vary widely; whether this variation reflects how cognitive outcomes are ascertained is unknown. Objective: To examine whether associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident cognitive impairment vary by outcome ascertainment rigor. Design, Setting, and Participants: This harmonized cohort study included 91,043 adults aged 50 years or older from 4 national longitudinal aging cohorts (CHARLS [China], HRS [US], ELSA [England], and SHARE [16 European countries]); baseline waves spanned 2006 to 2011, with follow-up through 2023. Exposure: Depressive symptom trajectory classes (persistent low, persistent high, incident worsening, remitting) derived using group-based trajectory modeling. Main Outcomes and Measures: Incident cognitive impairment ascertained under a 5-level hierarchy of increasing rigor, from self-report (level 1) to clinical consensus diagnosis (level 5; Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol [HCAP]). Cohort-specific Cox models were pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; meta-regression tested ascertainment rigor as a moderator of heterogeneity. Results: Under nonadjudicated outcomes, the incident-worsening trajectory was associated with incident cognitive impairment in CHARLS (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.06-1.62) and SHARE (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.87-2.13) but not HRS (HR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.95-1.16) or ELSA (HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.95-1.27); the persistent-high trajectory was not significant under any nonadjudicated outcome (HR range, 1.07-1.15). Under clinical consensus diagnosis (n = 3,196), all non-low trajectories were independently associated with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (OR range, 1.66-2.29; dementia-only persistent high: OR, 3.32; 95% CI, 1.85-5.95). Effect sizes increased stepwise with ascertainment rigor (meta-regression slope, 0.314 log HR per level; P < .001; residual I2 = 0%; R2 = 100%; exploratory). Findings were robust to lagged, weighted, and competing-risk analyses; biological aging acceleration did not differ across trajectories. Conclusions and Relevance: The detectability and magnitude of depression-related cognitive risk depend on outcome ascertainment rigor. Prevention trials and burden projections relying on self-reported outcomes may underestimate the benefit of depression treatment.

papers.title: Elevated maternal hemoglobin levels during pregnancy are associated with autism spectrum disorder in the offspring: A population-based cohort study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368133 v1

summary.background:
- Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): a neurodevelopmental condition affecting social communication and behavior; diagnosed from medical records here.
- Hemoglobin (Hb): the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells; measured in routine prenatal blood tests.
- Anemia: low hemoglobin; prior research links it to worse offspring neurodevelopment.
- Trimesters: the three roughly three-month stages of pregnancy.
- Cohort study: follows a defined group over time to see who develops an outcome.
- Adjusted odds ratio (aOR): a measure of how much more likely an outcome is in one group versus a reference group, after accounting for other factors; 1.22 means about 22% higher odds.
- Sibling-matched analysis: compares siblings from the same mother to reduce the influence of shared family factors.
- Limitations noted by authors: no data on maternal smoking or detailed nutrition; population is Jewish mothers in one HMO.
summary.one_liner: A large Israeli health-records cohort (303,234 singleton births, 2011–2021) found that high maternal hemoglobin in the first or second trimester was associated with higher odds of a later autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis in offspring, with the strongest signal for first-trimester values.
summary.plain: Researchers looked at whether a mother's blood hemoglobin level during pregnancy, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, is linked to whether her child later receives an autism diagnosis. Using electronic medical records from one large Israeli health organization, they compared children whose mothers had unusually high hemoglobin readings with children whose mothers had typical readings. They found that high readings were associated with somewhat higher odds of an autism diagnosis, though this is an association and does not show that high hemoglobin causes autism.
summary.why: Most prenatal blood research has focused on low hemoglobin (anemia), so the question of whether unusually high levels matter is less explored. The result is worth following up, but it comes from one observational study, and the authors themselves call for replication and for clarifying the biological mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an increasingly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition with multifactorial origins, including potential prenatal environmental contributions. Maternal anemia (decreased hemoglobin [Hb] levels) has long been associated with adverse offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes. Yet, evidence regarding elevated levels of antenatal hemoglobin levels, in relation to ASD risk remains limited. This study evaluated the association between maternal Hb levels during pregnancy and the risk of ASD diagnosis in offspring. Methods This large-scale, population-based retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from births of members of Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, between 2011 and 2021. The study included 303,234 singleton live births to Jewish mothers who had at least one measured prenatal Hb value and were CHS members. Exclusion criteria were children with known genetic disorders and births <25 weeks of gestation. Maternal Hb, and red blood cells (RBC) levels during the first and second trimesters were categorized as low (<2.5th percentile), normal (reference), or high (>97.5th percentile). The main outcome was a diagnosis of ASD in the offspring, as recorded in medical files. Statistical analyses adjusted for maternal age, socioeconomic status, gestational diabetes, BMI, and other clinical and demographic factors. Results Among the 303,234 births, 8,106 (2.7%) children were diagnosed with ASD. High maternal Hb levels were associated with elevated odds of ASD diagnosis (aOR=1.22; 95% CI=1.08:1.37), with the strongest association observed for first-trimester measurements (aOR=1.31; 95% CI=1.14-1.49). This association persisted in the sibling-matched analysis (aOR=1.64; 95% CI=1.08-2.47) and was not modified by maternal RBC levels, suggesting that it was not explained by familial factors or RBC counts. The main limitations of this study include the lack of available data on maternal smoking, and the absence of detailed information on maternal nutritional status. Conclusions These findings suggest that elevated antenatal Hb levels may be relevant to offspring neurodevelopment. Further studies are needed to replicate these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying this association.

papers.title: Chronic Maternal White Blood Cell Elevation During Pregnancy and Offspring Autism
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368136 v1

summary.background:
- Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): a neurodevelopmental condition diagnosed through clinical assessment; here, diagnoses recorded in health records.
- Maternal immune activation hypothesis: the idea that immune activity in a pregnant woman can affect the developing brain of the fetus.
- White blood cells (WBCs): immune cells in the blood; total counts and subtypes (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes) are routinely measured in prenatal care.
- Odds ratio (OR): how much the odds of an outcome change for an exposure; 1.59 means roughly 59% higher odds, not a 59% higher probability.
- Retrospective cohort: following existing health records over time rather than enrolling and following participants forward.
- Matched-sibling analysis: comparing siblings born to the same mother with different exposures, which helps control for shared family factors.
- Chronicity analysis: checking whether the same mother had high counts across multiple pregnancies.
- Percentiles: high and low exposures were defined as the top and bottom 2.5% of counts.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective Israeli cohort of 303,234 singleton births finds that elevated maternal white blood cell counts from routine first- and second-trimester tests are associated with higher odds of clinically diagnosed autism, with weaker support from sibling-matched and repeated-pregnancy analyses.
summary.plain: Autism is linked to the mother's immune system during pregnancy, but the specialized immune tests used in past studies are not part of routine care. This study checked whether ordinary blood counts (white blood cells, which fight infection) taken during pregnancy relate to a child's later autism diagnosis. It found that mothers with unusually high counts had somewhat higher odds of having an autistic child, and that this was most visible when the counts were high across several pregnancies.
summary.why: If routine blood counts carry a real signal, they could be used cheaply across whole populations to help flag pregnancies at higher risk, and they add support to the idea that maternal immune activation plays a role in autism. The text does not show that the counts cause autism, and most associations shrank in the sibling comparison, so the link is best treated as an association that needs confirmation.

papers.abstract: Background: Maternal immune activation is a robust risk factor for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current evidence relies on specialized immunological markers not routinely measured, limiting population-level risk identification. We investigated the association between maternal white blood cell (WBC) counts, a ubiquitous component of routine prenatal care during pregnancy, and offspring ASD risk. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study of 303,234 singleton live births (51% male) between 2011 and 2021 from Clalit Health Services in Israel. Exposures were maternal total and differential WBC counts from routine testing during the 1st and 2nd trimesters. High and low exposures were defined as >97.5th and <2.5th percentiles, respectively. The primary outcome was clinical ASD diagnosis. Analyses included multivariable logistic regressions, matched-sibling analyses (n=2,894 discordant pairs), and chronicity analyses in multiparous mothers (n=72,102). Results: Among 303,234 children, 8,106 (2.7%) were diagnosed with ASD. Elevated maternal total WBC counts were associated with increased odds of ASD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=1.59; 95% CI, 1.43-1.75), with the strongest association in the 1st trimester (aOR=1.64; 95% CI, 1.45-1.85). Similar associations were seen with elevated neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes. While most associations were attenuated in matched-sibling analyses, chronicity analysis revealed increased ASD odds in offspring of mothers with persistently elevated WBC counts across multiple pregnancies (aOR=1.49; 95% CI, 1.08-2.01). Conclusions: Persistently elevated maternal WBC counts across pregnancies are associated with increased offspring ASD risk. These routinely collected hematologic markers support the maternal immune activation hypothesis and may contribute to future prenatal risk assessment models.

papers.title: Perinatal suicide risk factors: A network analysis
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368387 v1

summary.background:
- Perinatal period: pregnancy and the first year after birth.
- National Violent Death Reporting System: a US database of details gathered from death investigations and records.
- Cross-sectional study: a snapshot of many cases at one point in the data, which cannot establish cause and effect.
- Network analysis: a method that treats each factor as a point and each statistical association as a line, showing which factors cluster together.
- Bridge centrality: how strongly a factor links otherwise separate clusters of factors.
- Network stability: whether the map holds up when the data are slightly resampled. The paper reports the overall network as stable and the perinatal network as only modestly stable, which means its details deserve more caution.
- Binary indicator: a yes-or-no record of whether a circumstance was present.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional psychometric network analysis of 2003–2023 National Violent Death Reporting System suicide decedents (N=20,217) comparing 18 binary life-circumstance indicators between perinatal and non-perinatal women, with attention to bridge centrality and network stability.
summary.plain: This paper looks at women who died by suicide while pregnant or within the first year after giving birth, a period that is a leading preventable cause of maternal death in the United States. Using death records from 2003 to 2023, the researchers mapped how 18 everyday circumstances, such as relationship problems, health issues, money troubles, and known suicide risk factors, tend to occur together. They then compared that map for perinatal deaths (1,297 cases) with the map for all other deaths (18,920 cases).
summary.why: Maternal suicide is a preventable cause of death, and the paper suggests that prevention for women of childbearing age should look beyond pregnancy itself to health, partner relationships, and finances. The findings describe associations in death records, not causes, so they point to where prevention might focus rather than proving what works.

papers.abstract: Purpose Suicide during pregnancy or after birth (the perinatal period) represents a leading, preventable cause of United States maternal deaths. This study aimed to understand the complex relationship between perinatal status and life circumstances among perinatal suicide decedents in the United States and generate insights regarding suicide risk. Methods This cross-sectional study used decedent data from the 2003-2023 National Violent Death Reporting System suicide mortality registry (N=20,217). We applied psychometric network analysis using 18 binary life circumstances indicators representing four domains: relationships, health, socioeconomic status, and risk factors for suicide. We generated two networks for the overall sample and perinatal sample and assessed network structure, bridge centralities, and stability. Results The analytic sample included 1,297 perinatal and 18,920 non-perinatal decedents. The network of the overall sample was stable. Perinatal status did not appear at the center of the network but connected primarily with intimate partner problems. The network of the perinatal sample was modestly stable. Postpartum status was not at the center of the network but connected to depressed mood and mental health diagnoses. In both networks, depressed mood had the highest bridge betweenness, and there was a consistent link between physical health domains and socioeconomic domains. Conclusion Suicide prevention strategies targeting childbearing-aged women should incorporate factors beyond pregnancy, including physical health, intimate partner relationships, and socioeconomic challenges.

papers.title: Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, longitudinal blood pressure trajectories, and hypertension-related outcomes in older adults at high cardiovascular risk: a cohort study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368306 v1

summary.background:
- PREDIMED was a large Spanish trial testing Mediterranean-style diets in people at high cardiovascular risk; this paper analyses its data.
- Blood pressure is reported as two numbers: systolic (pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (pressure between beats). High blood pressure here means above 140 or 90 mmHg.
- Physical activity was self-reported with a questionnaire and summarised as MET-minutes per day (MET is a unit of activity intensity); over 100 MET-minutes/day was labelled "adequate".
- Mixed-effects models track repeated measurements in each person over time; Cox models estimate the relative rate of an event (hazard ratio, HR) over follow-up. An HR below 1 means a lower rate of the event.
- Observational cohort findings show association, not cause.
summary.one_liner: In a secondary analysis of the PREDIMED trial (5,254 adults aged 60-80 at high cardiovascular risk), higher moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time physical activity was not linked to clinically meaningful differences in blood pressure trajectories or new high blood pressure, but was associated with lower risk of starting antihypertensive drugs, with a possible sex difference.
summary.plain: This study asks whether being more physically active in your free time, such as brisk walking, cycling or sports at a moderate-to-vigorous effort, is linked to healthier blood pressure in older adults who already face high heart risk. The researchers followed over 5,000 people over time and tracked their blood pressure, new high blood pressure diagnoses, and when they began taking blood pressure medication. Activity did not change blood pressure readings in a meaningful way or the chance of new high blood pressure, but people who were more active were less likely to start blood pressure medicine.
summary.why: Starting blood pressure medication is a practical, clinically important event, so a link to activity suggests exercise may matter in day-to-day cardiovascular care. The sex difference was not clearly established (interaction p = 0.058), so it should be treated as a hint rather than a finding, and the study is observational, so it cannot prove activity caused the difference.

papers.abstract: Background: We aimed to investigate the association between moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time physical activity (MVLTPA) and longitudinal trajectories of systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure, as well as the incidence of high blood pressure and antihypertensive drug initiation, in adults aged 60-80 years at high cardiovascular risk. Methods: In participants from the PREDIMED trial (61% women; 5,254 participants), MVLTPA was assessed using the Minnesota Leisure Time Physical Activity Questionnaire and expressed as cumulative average metabolic equivalent of task-minutes/day. SBP and DBP trajectories were modelled using mixed-effects models with cubic splines (>100 [adequate] vs <100 [insufficient] metabolic equivalent of task-minutes/day). First occurrence of high blood pressure (SBP >140 mmHg or DBP >90 mmHg) and antihypertensive drug initiation were assessed with Cox models (adequate vs insufficient, and continuous MVLTPA). Results: SBP and DBP declined with increasing age, with no clinically meaningful differences between MVLTPA groups. The association between adequate MVLTPA and incident high blood pressure was null (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.94-1.32). However, adequate MVLTPA was associated with a 17% lower risk of antihypertensive drug initiation (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.98). The association appeared stronger in women (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) than in men (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78-1.22) (p-value for sex interaction = 0.058). A modest inverse linear dose-response association between MVLTPA and risk of antihypertensive drug initiation was also observed (per 25 metabolic equivalent of task-minutes/day: HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.97-1.00; p-value = 0.022). Conclusions: In older adults at high cardiovascular risk, MVLTPA was not associated with clinically meaningful differences in SBP or DBP trajectories or incident high blood pressure, but was associated with a lower risk of antihypertensive drug initiation. These findings support promoting habitual physical activity as part of cardiovascular risk management in older adults.

papers.title: The plateau in liver disease mortality in Germany: contrasting trends by age, region and ICD-10 code, 2000-2024
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368157 v1

summary.background:
- Cirrhosis: scarring of the liver, often found only when it causes complications (decompensation).
- Age-standardised rate: a death rate adjusted to a standard age structure so populations can be compared fairly.
- ICD-10: the international coding system doctors and registries use to classify causes of death; K70–K77 covers liver disease, K74.6 is "unspecified cirrhosis."
- Birth cohort: a group of people born in the same years; comparing cohorts helps separate lifetime exposures from calendar-year effects.
- Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023: a modelled global estimate that assigns liver deaths to causes such as alcohol, viral hepatitis, and metabolic disease, partly using statistical models rather than recorded causes.
- Case fatality: the share of hospitalised patients who die during that stay.
summary.one_liner: A registry-based analysis of German and European liver disease mortality (2000–2024) by age, sex, federal state and detailed ICD-10 code, compared with Global Burden of Disease 2023 aetiology estimates, finds that Germany's cirrhosis mortality plateau reflects rising deaths at ages 65–74, concentrated in unspecified cirrhosis (K74.6) and in eastern Germany.
summary.plain: Germany's death rate from chronic liver disease has stopped falling while several neighbouring countries' rates have dropped. This paper looks at death certificates, hospital records and modelled global estimates to find where the plateau comes from. The authors report that deaths are still falling under age 65 but are rising among people aged 65 to 74, especially in the east, and that most of these cirrhosis deaths are recorded without a stated cause.
summary.why: The findings point to older cohorts with high past alcohol exposure as a possible driver, and suggest that older adults may need earlier detection and better treatment access. The authors also warn that global models assigning causes to cirrhosis deaths cannot be checked against routine death registration data, so those cause-specific figures should be read cautiously.

papers.abstract: BackgroundCirrhosis is often diagnosed only at decompensation, making identification of high-risk groups important for prevention and early detection. Chronic liver disease mortality has fallen in southern Europe and France since 2010, but not in Germany. Whether the German plateau reflects birth-cohort alcohol exposure, metabolic liver disease or certification practice is unknown. MethodsDeaths by ICD-10 code, sex and age group were extracted from the WHO Mortality Database for 16 European countries (2000-2022), with Eurostat rates (2011-2023), German state-level mortality (1998-2024) and hospital diagnoses (2000-2023). Registry and Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023 estimates were summarised for ages 45-64, 65-74 and 75 years and over, with registry rates standardised to the European Standard Population 2013. FindingsGermanys age-standardised chronic liver disease mortality was 16.6 per 100 000 in 2011 and 16.0 in 2023, against declines of 21-37% in France, Italy and Spain. Between 2010 and 2022, alcoholic liver disease mortality at ages 45-64 fell by 17% in men and 25% in women, whereas fibrosis and cirrhosis (K74) mortality at ages 65-74 rose by 27% and 28%, with larger K70-K77 mortality increases in eastern than western Germany. Hospitalisation rates showed similar age-specific patterns, while in-hospital case fatality declined. Fewer than 0.5% of liver deaths were certified as fatty liver. GBD 2023 showed a similar age-specific increase but attributed rising mortality to all five modelled aetiologies. InterpretationThe German plateau reflects continued decline below age 65 and rising mortality at ages 65-74, compatible with cohorts born 1945-59 reaching this age band, particularly in eastern Germany. Consumption records and surveys indicate differing regional patterns of alcohol exposure. Much of the cirrhosis in these cohorts is certified without aetiology, and GBDs aetiological estimates cannot be verified in registration data. FundingNone. Research in context Evidence before this studyPubMed was searched without language restriction from inception to October 15, 2026, for registry-based analyses of cirrhosis or chronic liver disease mortality in Germany or in European comparisons, and for comparisons of GBD estimates with vital registration, using combinations of the terms cirrhosis, liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease, mortality, Germany, Europe, age-period-cohort, Global Burden of Disease and vital registration. Registry analyses have documented an east-to-west gradient of cirrhosis mortality across Europe and, in Germany, period and birth-cohort effects on alcohol-related mortality, with lower risks in later-born cohorts. A nationwide hospital study reported rising admissions for cirrhosis with falling in-hospital mortality. GBD publications acknowledge that ICD coding cannot reliably distinguish cirrhosis aetiologies, which are assigned using statistical models. We found no previous study combining detailed ICD-10 mortality analyses, age-specific European comparison, German federal-state trends and comparison with GBD aetiological estimates. Added value of this studyWe compared GBD 2023 estimates with European mortality registration data and examined German mortality by detailed ICD-10 code, age, sex and federal state, alongside hospital diagnosis statistics. The German plateau reflects rising mortality at 65-74 years, especially in eastern Germany, while mortality continues to decline at 45-64 years. The increase was concentrated in deaths coded as unspecified cirrhosis (K74.6) and accompanied by rising cirrhosis hospitalisation rates. At the same time, in-hospital case fatality and admissions for chronic viral hepatitis declined. GBD identified a similar age-specific increase but estimated rising mortality for all five aetiological sub-causes despite their differing representation in routine data. Implications of all the available evidenceThe absence of a decline in cirrhosis mortality in Germany is consistent with older birth cohorts with high cumulative alcohol exposure, although the aetiology of cirrhosis is often unspecified. Differences in alcohol consumption patterns, obesity and conditions after reunification may contribute to higher mortality in parts of eastern Germany. The findings support earlier detection and improved treatment access for older adults, age-specific surveillance in Germany and other European countries, and cautious interpretation of modelled aetiological fractions in countries without multiple-cause mortality data.

papers.title: Influenza activity in the United States during the 2025-26 influenza season
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26367927 v1

summary.background:
- Influenza (flu) is a common respiratory virus; A and B are its main types for seasonal epidemics.
- Subclades are finer genetic groupings within a flu type; H3N2 is a specific A-type subtype.
- "Antigenically drifted" means the virus's surface proteins have changed enough that vaccine-induced immunity may match it less well.
- Vaccines are chosen each year from reference strains predicted to match the upcoming season's viruses.
- Surveillance means ongoing collection of case, hospital and death data to track disease.
- The severity rating here uses CDC's established framework, which grades the season as low, moderate or high for each age group.
- The text gives a data window ending October 3, 2026 and a pediatric death count as of October 29, 2026, which is inconsistent with a 2025-26 season report; readers should check these dates against the original source.
summary.one_liner: CDC's season summary of U.S. influenza activity for 2025-26, covering timing, two epidemic waves, dominant A(H3N2) subclade K viruses, vaccine mismatch, age-specific severity, and pediatric deaths.
summary.plain: This is an official government report on how the flu season went in the United States from late September 2025 onward. It tracks lab test results, doctor and emergency room visits, hospital stays and deaths, then rates how severe the season was. The main findings are that flu peaked in late December 2025, earlier than the previous season, and that a strain called A(H3N2) subclade K dominated, with a smaller second wave of a B-type strain.
summary.why: The report flags that children had their highest cumulative flu hospitalization rate in 16 years and that most circulating viruses differed antigenically from the vaccine strains, which matters for vaccine planning and child health. The text itself concludes the season was within historic norms for timing and severity, so the child-specific findings are the main point of interest.

papers.abstract: BackgroundComprehensive influenza surveillance is conducted year-round in the United States to monitor changes in influenza activity. This report summarizes the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season. MethodsData from September 28, 2025 through October 3, 2026 were collected from national surveillance systems monitoring influenza through laboratory testing, outpatient and emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and mortality. Data modeled disease burden and assessed severity using established criteria. A subset of influenza positive specimens were genetically and antigenically characterized and assessed for antiviral susceptibility. ResultsInfluenza activity peaked during the week ending December 27, 2025, five weeks earlier than the 2024-25 season. There were two waves of influenza activity with influenza A(H3N2) subclade K viruses predominating the season overall and during the first wave followed by a smaller B/Victoria wave. The majority of circulating A(H3N2) and B/Victoria viruses were antigenically drifted from 2025-26 influenza vaccine reference strains. Season severity was classified as moderate overall, with children (0-17 years old) experiencing a high severity season and adults experiencing a moderate severity season. Children experienced the highest percent of influenza-associated outpatient and emergency department visits compared to other age groups. This seasons cumulative influenza-associated hospitalization rate in children is the highest hospitalization rate in the past 16 years. Additionally, there were 198 influenza-associated pediatric deaths reported to CDC as of October 29, 2026. ConclusionsAlthough antigenically drifted A(H3N2) viruses predominated, the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season occurred within historic norms for timing and severity. Year-round surveillance remains critical for detecting changes in influenza viruses and monitoring influenza-associated morbidity and mortality.
